newsitem.title: USA: Shifting US/Japan rate prospects push dollar lower.
newsitem.headline: Shifting US/Japan rate prospects push dollar lower.

text.p: The dollar fell sharply against the Japanese yen and other major currencies on Friday after Japanese officials warned of intervention to curb its strength as speculation mounted that Japan would soon raise interest rates.
A speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Thursday night in New York also weighed on the dollar by suggesting that the U.S. central bank may put off further hikes in U.S. interest rates.

The dollar slipped against the yen for the fifth consecutive day, by over four-and-a-half yen at its lowest point of the day -- the largest intra-day retreat against the Japanese currency since September 1995.
The dollar ended the day at 120.20 yen, down from 123.75 late Thursday. It fell to 1.6875 German marks, down more than two pfennings from Thursday's closing rate of 1.7085.

Until this week, the dollar had been supported by expectations of higher U.S. rates and continued low rates in Japan. Higher rates tend to bolster a country's currency by making its bonds and other assets relatively more attractive.
But Greenspan's speech and a Japanese newspaper report led traders to reevaluate these rate expectations and send the dollar lower Friday.
The U.S. central bank chief said late Thursday that he expected growth to slow later this year and cited only scant signs of a resurgence of inflation.

"The ball started rolling with Greenspan," said Bob Near, vice president on the corporate foreign exchange desk at Bank of New York. "The market consensus was that he was telling us he was not going to hike on May 20."
In contrast, a report in Japanese newspaper Nikkei Kinyu hinted of higher rates in Japan by noting that talk of a July interest rate hike was behind rising Japanese government bond yields.
Also hurting the dollar were remarks from Japanese monetary authorities, who continued to talk the dollar lower.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka was quoted on Friday as saying that intervention in foreign exchange markets should be done jointly with other nations, and influential Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara said Japan would deal with excessive movements in the currency markets decisively and in a timely manner.
"Shifting interest rate expectations are occuring in Japan alongside repeated concerns about yen weakness voiced by Japanese officials," said Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International.
The dollar retreated sharply to 1.4235 Swiss francs from 1.4450 late Thursday. It slid to $1.6225.British pounds from $1.6200. The dollar rose Canadian $1.3920 from C$1.3862.
